name: Ureters
func: Two thin muscular tubes that carry urine from each kidney down to the bladder. Waves of muscle squeezing push urine along, and a one-way valve stops it flowing back up.

levels.kid:
Your **ureters** are two long, skinny tubes, a bit thinner than a drinking straw. One comes out of each kidney.

When your kidneys make pee, the pee needs a way to get to your bladder, the stretchy bag low in your tummy. The ureters are that road.

The cool part is that the pee doesn't just drip down. The walls of the ureters squeeze, squeeze, squeeze in little waves, like when you push toothpaste along a tube. That means pee can even get to your bladder when you're lying down or standing on your head!

Where the ureters join the bladder there is a little flap, like a door that only opens one way, so pee can't go back up.
levels.hs:
The **ureters** are paired muscular tubes about 25–30 cm long and 3–4 mm wide. Each begins at the **renal pelvis** of the kidney, runs down the back wall of the abdomen on top of the **psoas major** muscle, crosses into the pelvis over the **common iliac artery** near where it splits, and enters the back of the **bladder**.

They are **retroperitoneal**, lying behind the abdominal lining, roughly in line with the tips of the lumbar vertebrae's transverse processes. The right ureter runs near the inferior vena cava and the left near the aorta.

Urine moves by **peristalsis**: smooth muscle in the wall contracts in waves a few times every minute, starting from pacemaker cells near the renal pelvis. Gravity helps but isn't needed.

Where each ureter enters the bladder, it tunnels at an angle through the bladder wall. When the bladder fills and stretches, this tunnel squeezes shut, acting as a **one-way valve**. This protects the kidneys from backflow of urine and infection.
levels.college:
Each ureter has an **abdominal** and a **pelvic** part. The wall has three layers: an inner **transitional epithelium (urothelium)** that stretches and resists urine, a **muscularis** (inner longitudinal and outer circular in the upper ureter, with an extra outer longitudinal layer lower down), and an outer **adventitia**.

Three classic **narrowings** are where stones lodge: the **pelviureteric junction (PUJ)**, the **pelvic brim** where the ureter crosses the iliac vessels, and the **vesicoureteric junction (VUJ)**, the narrowest point.

**Blood supply** is segmental from nearby vessels: renal artery above, then branches from the aorta and common iliac artery, then the internal iliac branches (superior and inferior vesical arteries) in the pelvis. Because the vessels approach from the medial side in the abdomen and the lateral side in the pelvis, surgeons mobilise the ureter accordingly to protect its blood supply.

**Pain** from a ureter travels in sympathetic fibres to spinal segments roughly T11–L2, so pain is referred from the loin toward the groin and front of the thigh, moving downward as a stone descends.

The ureter is closely related to the **sigmoid mesocolon** on the left and the **ileocaecal region** on the right, which matters in bowel surgery.
levels.phd:
Ureteric peristalsis is myogenic. **Atypical smooth muscle cells** at the renal pelvis and pelviureteric junction act as pacemakers, and **interstitial cells of Cajal-like cells** help couple and propagate the signal. Electrical activity spreads cell-to-cell through gap junctions; contraction depends on L-type calcium channels and calcium-activated chloride currents, with relaxation through potassium channels. Nerves modulate but don't generate peristalsis, which is why a transplanted, denervated ureter still works.

The **urothelium** is a three-layered epithelium. Its large **umbrella cells** carry plaques of **uroplakins** (UPIa, UPIb, UPII, UPIIIa) that form an asymmetric unit membrane with very low permeability to water and urea. Fusiform vesicles let umbrella cells add membrane as the tube stretches. The urothelium is also a sensor, releasing **ATP** onto P2X3 receptors on afferent nerves when stretched.

In development, the ureter grows as the **ureteric bud** from the mesonephric duct; GDNF from the metanephric mesenchyme acting on **RET** receptors drives branching that forms the whole collecting system. Errors in where the bud arises cause **duplex ureters**, ectopic ureters and abnormal valve tunnels that lead to reflux. SHH and BMP4 signalling pattern the smooth muscle coat, and defects can cause functional obstruction such as **megaureter**.
levels.expert:
The classic presentation of a ureteric stone is **renal colic**: sudden, severe, colicky loin-to-groin pain, often with nausea, restlessness (unlike peritonitis, where patients lie still) and **haematuria** on dipstick. Fever with an obstructed kidney is an emergency (**infected obstructed kidney**) needing urgent drainage by **ureteric stent** or **percutaneous nephrostomy**.

**Imaging**: non-contrast **CT KUB** is the gold standard and shows stones and hydroureter; ultrasound is used to avoid radiation in children. On CT, a **soft-tissue rim sign** around a stone helps separate it from a phlebolith (a calcified pelvic vein, which shows a comet-tail sign instead). Small stones often pass on their own; larger ones are treated by **ureteroscopy** with laser fragmentation or shockwave lithotripsy.

**Vesicoureteric reflux** in children is graded I–V on a micturating cystourethrogram and can scar the kidneys after infections. **PUJ obstruction** is a common cause of congenital hydronephrosis and is repaired by pyeloplasty.

The ureter is one of the most commonly injured structures in **pelvic and colorectal surgery**, especially near the pelvic brim. Surgeons identify it by its **vermiculation** (visible worm-like peristalsis when touched) and often place stents before difficult operations. Retroperitoneal fibrosis and pelvic tumours can trap and obstruct the ureters from outside.

keyPoints: ~25–30 cm muscular tubes from renal pelvis to bladder
Run on psoas, cross the iliac vessels at the pelvic brim
Urine moves by peristalsis, not just gravity
Three narrowings where stones stick: PUJ, pelvic brim, VUJ (narrowest)
Oblique entry into the bladder wall acts as a one-way valve

test.q: Which is the narrowest point of the ureter, where stones most often get stuck?
test.explain: The vesicoureteric junction, where the ureter tunnels through the bladder wall, is the narrowest.

test.q: Urine moves down the ureter by waves of smooth muscle contraction called ______.
test.explain: Peristalsis starts from pacemaker cells near the renal pelvis.

test.q: What lining epithelium is found in the ureter?
test.explain: Urothelium stretches and is nearly waterproof thanks to uroplakin plaques.

test.q: Which artery does the ureter cross as it enters the pelvis?
test.explain: The ureter crosses the pelvic brim over the common iliac bifurcation.

test.q: What is the gold-standard scan for a suspected ureteric stone (3 letters + 3 letters)?
test.explain: Non-contrast CT of kidneys, ureters and bladder detects almost all stones.
